style.name: K1-minimal · house look (locked 2026-10-15)
style.block: A 2D key frame from a narrated animated film, drawn in this art style: our own K1 paper-cut look made minimal, the house look, as the reference image shows it. Every figure and prop is a few flat cut-paper shapes. Every figure and prop has a thick warm dark-brown ink outline and a thin light inner edge just inside it, and is creased once by a single straight diagonal line at the light's angle, its far side a deeper hue of its own colour turned toward violet, never grey and never black. A head is ONE simple shape inside one single thick outline, and the light inner edge runs round that one outline. Garments are flat planes: no pockets, no buttons, no stitching, no seams, no cuffs, no fabric texture. Hands are plain round paper circles at the end of each arm in its sleeve, the sleeve running from the shoulder to the hand: never a hand floating free of the body, never a bare arm, no thumbs, no fingers. Faces are three marks only: two small dark ink oval eyes, short brows and a one-line mouth. One muted hue per piece. The light and the place: a warm, soft key light from the upper left that falls in soft, hazy beams; a real place behind the figures, built of simple flat paper planes with no ink outline, each plane further back paler and softer in a warm haze, so depth comes from haze and never from blur; a soft paper grain on every piece and every plane; soft violet cast shadows on the walls and the floor, never a darker brown; a muted, warm palette in which only the film's accents are loud. Keep it K1: no white sticker border round the figures, no felt or stitching style, no big glossy eyes, no realistic anatomy. The look is stylised, attractive, expressive and minimal.
style.world: Righteousness by Faith, a narrated explainer film about how God makes people righteous: His word is a seed, not a label. It has two registers: an IDEA beat is a light parchment page with figures and props cut from paper laid on it; a STORY beat is a cardboard diorama of three to five layered paper planes under a simple two- or three-stop gradient sky, a real place in a soft haze. The film's plain lead, the accused in its parable of a courtroom (the parable's "a man", in whom any viewer can see himself), is one small figure cut from one pale cool grey paper with a faint lilac cast: a round head with no hair, no ears, no nose and no neck, sitting right on a plain trapezoid tunic that widens to a straight hem, two short rounded stub legs, two circle hands at the ends of his arms in their sleeves, never floating free of him, and a face of two short arched brows, two small dark dot eyes and a one-line mouth; his head is nearly as wide as his hem, and he is about 2.6 heads tall; nothing on him tells who he is. He keeps his height, build, paper and tunic in every frame; only at the landing is his tunic made white. His courtroom: a cream wall with pale columns and a teal dado, one high window, a wooden dock at screen-left whose front rail crosses his tunic two thirds down, a small wooden table for the prosecutor in the middle, and the judge's tall wooden bench at screen-right with a gavel on its block; the top of the accused's head is level with the top of the bench. The judge is a grey-haired older man in a dark robe with white bands; the prosecutor is a man a head taller than the accused, with jet-black hair, in an olive tunic. A second plain figure, a grandmother, is the same figure as the lead in a warm oat paper. The Bible's scenes are peopled by men and women of the ancient Near East in plain undyed linen, walnut, indigo and olive cloth, of varied heights, builds and headcloths, never clones. Jesus is an ordinary Jewish man with short dark hair and a short dark beard, in a plain white robe with a gold sash, with no halo. The colour script: scarlet only for sin (stains), white only for the robe, gold only for God's word and gift (the seal, the seed); everything else calm creams, taupes, teals and peaches.

Screen direction holds for the film: the accused screen-left, the bench screen-right. THIS PANEL: The accused stands in the dock screen-left with the scarlet stain on the front of his tunic and no gold seal yet (it comes later). THE MOMENT: this frame holds from the narrator's words «Every piece of evidence says one…»: draw what the brief has on screen at that moment, and nothing the brief brings in later.

TEXT: no captions, no subtitles, no narration, no titles, no speech bubbles, no signatures and no labels anywhere. Where the brief names a word card, a title, a question or a verse being written or shown, leave it out: the film sets every spoken word as a full-screen card of its own. The only letters allowed are one short word the brief puts on a prop in this moment (a stamp, a sign), spelled exactly; otherwise no letters or numbers at all, and any paper, book or tablet in the frame is blank or shows only soft unreadable lines.

RULES: Shade with colour: every shaded side and every cast shadow turns its hue toward the complement of the light (violet-blue under a warm light), never black and never plain grey; outlines may be dark. Hands are plain round circles: no thumbs, no fingers. No crosses on buildings, church buildings, religious symbols, logos or emblems anywhere, unless the brief names one. The second reference image is the film's kept frame of the landing: the cold open's courtroom changed, in its bright teal day: keep its place, its set pieces, its people as they look there, their colours and its light, framed as this moment asks.

THE FILM'S WORLD: Righteousness by Faith, a narrated explainer film about how God makes people righteous: His word is a seed, not a label. It has two registers: an IDEA beat is a light parchment page with figures and props cut from paper laid on it; a STORY beat is a cardboard diorama of three to five layered paper planes under a simple two- or three-stop gradient sky, a real place in a soft haze. The film's plain lead, the accused in its parable of a courtroom (the parable's "a man", in whom any viewer can see himself), is one small figure cut from one pale cool grey paper with a faint lilac cast: a round head with no hair, no ears, no nose and no neck, sitting right on a plain trapezoid tunic that widens to a straight hem, two short rounded stub legs, two circle hands floating beside him, and a face of two short arched brows, two small dark dot eyes and a one-line mouth; his head is nearly as wide as his hem, and he is about 2.6 heads tall; nothing on him tells who he is. He keeps his height, build, paper and tunic in every frame; only at the landing is his tunic made white. His courtroom: a cream wall with pale columns and a teal dado, one high window, a wooden dock at screen-left whose front rail crosses his tunic two thirds down, a small wooden table for the prosecutor in the middle, and the judge's tall wooden bench at screen-right with a gavel on its block; the top of the accused's head is level with the top of the bench. The judge is a grey-haired older man in a dark robe with white bands; the prosecutor is a man a head taller than the accused, with jet-black hair, in an olive tunic. A second plain figure, a grandmother, is the same figure as the lead in a warm oat paper. The Bible's scenes are peopled by men and women of the ancient Near East in plain undyed linen, walnut, indigo and olive cloth, of varied heights, builds and headcloths, never clones. Jesus is an ordinary Jewish man with short dark hair and a short dark beard, in a plain white robe with a gold sash, with no halo.
